lectureMeta: The week's Readiness Assessment, as it was sat.
stem: What is the term for successful cellular response to stress?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Adaptation describes the different mechanisms cells can use to respond to stress / injury. The adaptive mechanisms are hyperplasia, hypertrophy, atrophy and metaplasia. Apoptosis is controlled / programmed cell death and necrosis is uncontrolled cell death, both of which may occur in response to irreversible cell injury. CDK inhibition is a mechanism of cell cycle inhibition whereby the cell cycle is delayed at certain checkpoints to check for DNA damage.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Body Fluids, Blood Pressure & Screening
lectureMeta: The week's Readiness Assessment, as it was sat.
stem: Which of the following mechanisms of cell death results in a host inflammatory response?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Apoptosis (programmed cell death) is a tightly regulated process, designed to avoid damage to the surrounding tissues. Necrosis involves loss of cell membrane integrity and spillage of cellular contents into the surrounding tissues, and results in an inflammatory response to clear up the damage.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Body Fluids, Blood Pressure & Screening
lectureMeta: The week's Readiness Assessment, as it was sat.
stem: Which of the following mechanisms of cell death results in a host inflammatory response?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

The immediate host inflammatory response involves dilation and opening of capillary beds, increased permeability of blood vessels, increased expression of endothelial adhesion molecules to attract and stop leukocytes, and contraction of endothelial cells in response to histamine to allow leukocytes to pass through inter-endothelial spaces into the surrounding tissues. Once recruited and activated, leukocytes become able to ingest microbes, dead cells and foreign material.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Even in tissues with regenerative capacity, if an injury is severe / large, healing is primarily by repair with scar formation, although some regeneration may also occur.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Permanent cells have very limited regenerative capacity. Tissues composed of permanent cells must therefore heal predominantly by repair, resulting in formation of a fibrous scar.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Body Fluids, Blood Pressure & Screening

stem: Excessive estrogen stimulation causes increased growth of endometrial glands
answer:
The correct answer is B.

From 05 - Cellular Stress & Repair. The four adaptations are told apart by what changes:

  • Hypertrophy - bigger cells, no new cells; the response of skeletal and cardiac muscle (limited division) to increased workload.
  • Hyperplasia - more cells, driven by hormones or growth factors, or compensatory after damage or resection.
  • Metaplasia - one mature tissue replaced by another not native to the site, a reversible response to chronic irritation.
  • Atrophy - loss of cell size and number; causes include disuse, denervation, diminished blood supply, poor nutrition, loss of endocrine stimulation, pressure.

Estrogen driving more endometrial glands is increased cell number in a hormone-sensitive organ under hormonal stimulation: hyperplasia. The glands multiply rather than simply enlarging, and they stay endometrium.

stem: Which of the following is not a complication of prolonged elevated blood pressure?
answer:

From 09 - Approach to Anxiety and Stress (charted as Effects of Stress and Inflammation on Blood Vessels). Sustained high pressure is hemodynamic stress on the endothelium; the vessel's repair response is intimal thickening, which narrows the lumen and cuts blood flow to the organ the vessel supplies. The complications are therefore vascular, organ by organ: atherosclerosis and MI, cardiac hypertrophy and heart failure, multi-infarct dementia, aortic dissection, cerebrovascular hemorrhage and renal failure.

  • B, C - renal failure and cerebrovascular disease are on the lecture's list.
  • A, E - erectile dysfunction and retinal hemorrhages are not named in the note, but they are the same small-vessel damage in the penile and retinal circulations.
  • D - cirrhosis is a disease of the liver parenchyma, not a consequence of arterial pressure.

stem: If you stand up suddenly after lying down for a long period of time, you can suddenly feel faint due to a decrease in blood pressure and blood flow to the brain. Which of the following mechanisms will occur rapidly through the baroreceptor reflex to return your blood pressure back to normal?

options.html: Decreasing heart rate and dilation of blood vessels
Decreasing heart rate and constriction of blood vessels
Increasing heart rate and constriction of blood vessels
Increasing heart rate and dilation of blood vessels
Decreasing heart rate and no change to blood vessels

answer:
The correct answer is C.

In order to return blood pressure (Mean arterial pressure or MAP) back to normal you must increase cardiac output (CO) and total peripheral resistance (TPR). Recall that MAP = CO x TPR. The baroreceptors in the carotid sinus detect the drop in MAP and they signal the cardiovascular center in the brainstem. This center, in turn, increase sympathetic output to the heart, which will increase both heart rate and stroke volume resulting in an increase in cardiac output. The cardiovascular center will also increase sympathetic output to the blood vessels (mainly arterioles) causing them to vasoconstrict. This will increase the total peripheral resistance, which will also help to increase MAP back to normal.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Body Fluids, Blood Pressure & Screening
lectureMeta: The week's Self-Assessment, as it was released.
stem: Which of the following is correct?

options.html: Vasoconstriction will lead to an increase in mean arterial pressure
The autonomic nervous system is generally under voluntary control
A decrease in stroke volume will cause an increase in MAP

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Constriction of a blood vessel will decrease the radius of the vessel. This will in turn increase the total peripheral resistance (TPR), the total resistance the blood will encounter in the systemic circulatory system. If TPR increases, we know that the mean arterial pressure (MAP) will also increase because it is directly related to TPR; Recall the equation MAP = Co x TPR (where CO = Cardiac Output). Therefore, when blood vessels in the peripheral circulation vasoconstrict, MAP will increase.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Body Fluids, Blood Pressure & Screening
lectureMeta: The week's Self-Assessment, as it was released.
stem: Which of the following hormones regulates blood pressure by indirectly increasing the reabsorption of sodium, promoting vasoconstriction and increasing thirst?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

The RAA pathway is activated when blood pressure drops. Aldosterone is the hormone that directly activate the mineralocorticoid receptors, leading in increased reabsorption of sodium by the kidney. Angiotensin II has the potential to increase sodium reabsorption by stimulating the secretion of aldosterone by the adrenal glands (indirect effect). Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor and acts in the hypothalamus, stimulating thirst via the release of ADH or vasopressin. Vasopressin can also promote vasoconstriction; however, its actions are focused on increasing water retention. Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) and B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) have opposite actions of angiotensin; these peptides promote vasodilation and promote natriuresis (sodium excretion).

weekLabel: Week 5 - Body Fluids, Blood Pressure & Screening
lectureMeta: The week's Self-Assessment, as it was released.
stem: Which of the following is correct concerning the baroreceptor reflex?

options.html: It relies on the release of hormones from the adrenal gland to cause vasodilation
High pressure receptors in the aortic arch and carotid sinus continuously monitor blood pressure
Signals from low pressure baroreceptors to the cardiovascular centre to monitor blood pressure and blood volume
The aortic arch detects low pressure conditions while the carotid sinuses detect high pressure conditions

answer:
The correct answer is B, C.

From 02 - Introduction to Blood Pressure Regulation. The baroreceptor reflex is a fast neural loop: stretch sensors send signals to the brain, which answers by changing heart rate or vessel diameter (TPR). High-pressure receptors sit in the aortic arch and carotid sinus and monitor blood pressure (B); low-pressure receptors sit in the atria and report blood volume to the same centre (C).

  • A - hormones are the slow arm of BP control; the reflex itself needs no adrenal hormone.
  • D - reversed: the aortic arch and carotid sinus are both high-pressure sites.
  • E - fails because A and D are false.

stem: A 49-year-old man develops blood clots in his right leg. If one of these were to break loose and flow through the venous system, it would embed in capillaries in which of the following locations?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Vascular drainage of the lower limbs is through the systemic veins into the right side of the heart. The right ventricle sends blood to the lungs, where the first capillary beds are encountered. Thus, the thrombus (blood clot) would lodge in the capillary beds of the lungs, producing a thromboembolism.

stem: A 49-year-old man presents with pain in his lower left abdomen and proximal medial thigh, but the pain also radiates to his left shoulder. Physical examination of the left shoulder reveals no structural abnormalities or weakness. The plain abdominal radiograph provided reveals a left renal and perirenal abscess. Which of the following organs is irritated by the abscess, resulting in the radiating pain to the left shoulder?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Superior spread of the abscess would cause visceral pain derived from the diaphragm because the diaphragm is closely related to the superior pole of the left kidney. The visceral sensory fibres conveying pain from the kidney are derived from the T12-L1 vertebral levels, which leads to referred pain in the lower abdomen and proximal medial thigh. Involvement of the diaphragm would refer pain to the left lower cervical and shoulder regions because the phrenic nerve, derived from vertebral levels C3-5, innervates the diaphragm.

stem: Clinical Scenario: Part 1 of 3 Nicola is a 28 year old breastfeeding mother to her 4 month old daughter. She complains of a lump in her right breast. It has been present for at least 3 months and she is worried that she has an abscess. There is no change in size or pain during / after breastfeeding. On examination there is a firm, mobile, non-tender mass in her right breast, measuring approximately 2.5 cm. Question 1: What are your initial steps in the clinic? Select 5

options.html: Ask if there is a family history of breast cancer

answer:
The correct answer is A, B, G, H, N.

Nipple discharge may be present if there is a duct problem (blocked duct / abscess, intraductal papilloma). A family history is important when dealing with a breast mass of uncertain etiology. If cancer is a concern, examining the abdomen for masses in the liver or hepatomegaly is part of clinical staging, although radiologic examination (usually by CT scan) is much more sensitive and specific. Axillary lymphadenopathy raises a red flag for malignancy, although it’s important to remember that lymph nodes may also be enlarged in infectious / inflammatory conditions. An enlarged node may be sampled by FNA. Taking her temperature as part of her vitals is important as mastitis / breast abscess may result in fever. Blood glucose and urine dipstick are irrelevant to her presenting complaint; punch biopsy is for skin lesions; doing nothing is not an option for a firm, non-tender mass; this needs to be investigated; broad infectious work up is not indicated for her presenting complaint; chest X-ray is not an appropriate test for examination of the breast tissue; there is no useful circulating tumour marker for breast cancer; a core needle biopsy is the appropriate diagnostic test so that the appropriate surgical procedure can be performed once the diagnosis is known, or so that no surgery is performed depending on the result; you would not refer to an oncologist without a confirmed diagnosis of cancer.

It has been present for at least 3 months and she is worried that she has an abscess. There is no change in size or pain during / after breastfeeding. On examination there is a firm, mobile, non-tender mass in her right breast, measuring approximately 2.5 cm. Question 2: What are your next steps? Select 2
answer:
The correct answer is B, I.

Ultrasound is the usual first line radiologic test for a breast mass and allows a targeted core needle biopsy to be performed. Mammogram is typically used for screening in an asymptomatic population. MRI is sometimes used to guide biopsy of a mass but this is used less commonly than ultrasound.

Question 3: Based on the clinical history and examination, what is the most likely diagnosis? Select 1
answer:
The correct answer is H.

From 04 - Diagnostic Pathway for Breast Mass. A firm, mobile, non-tender 2.5 cm mass in a 28-year-old, stable for months and unchanged by feeding, is the lecture's fibroadenoma: a benign single nodule, well circumscribed, firm and mobile. Young age already makes a benign cause most likely.

  • A, J - abscess and mastitis are common in breastfeeding, but they are warm, red, swollen and tender.
  • E - a cyst is a smooth fluid sac, not described as a firm solid mass.
  • I - carcinoma is usually hard, irregular and may be fixed, and is less likely at 28.
  • G, L - a node would sit in the axilla; normal lactation change is diffuse, not a discrete lump.
  • B, C, D, F, K, M, N - remaining VITAMIN C&D categories with nothing in the history to support them.

stem: Regarding cancer incidence and mortality statistics, which of the following statement(s) is/are true? i) Lung cancer is one of the most important causes of cancer death in both men and women in Canada ii) Cervical cancer is still a common cause of cancer death in women worldwide, but is not a frequent cancer anymore in Canadian women iii) Approximately 1 in 4 Canadians will die from cancer iv) A person in a high income country is more likely to be diagnosed with cancer in his/her lifetime than a person in a low income country. A person diagnosed with cancer in a high income country has a lower risk of dying of cancer than a person diagnosed with cancer in a low income country.

options.html: Only i) is a true statement
Only ii) is a true statement
Only i) and ii) are true statements
Only i), ii), and iii) are true statements
All of the above are true statements

answer:
The correct answer is E.

As outlined in the macro to micro large group discussion, the # 1 cause of cancer death in Canada is lung cancer, while cervical cancer is not frequent in Canada due to screening. 1 in 2 Canadians will be diagnosed with cancer, while 1 in 4 will die from it. High income countries diagnose cancer more likely related to the medical system, screening, access to care; while there is reduced mortality as well due to the medical system of care compared to low income countries. The other reason is that in low income countries many people do not reach an age where cancer manifests, since they die from infection, trauma, or other causes.

stem: Audrey develops colon cancer at age 43. She has a healthy brother and parents. Her maternal grandfather was diagnosed at age 60 with colon cancer. Her maternal grandmother’s brother has a daughter with colon cancer, diagnosed at age 50. She undergoes genetic testing for a panel of genes associated with colon cancer. Premature truncation of protein translation in any of the genes can cause colon cancer. Results are reported as: MSH2: c.1373T>G; p. L458X Which statement is true?

options.html: This is an example of genetic anticipation.
This is an example of autosomal recessive inheritance.
Audrey’s sister cannot be offered predictive genetic testing.
The amino acid change results in a substitution of xanthine.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

From 03 - Cancer Genetics. In p.L458X the “X” denotes a stop codon: leucine 458 is replaced by a premature stop, truncating the MSH2 protein. A point change that creates a stop is a nonsense mutation - the truncation the stem says causes colon cancer.

  • A - anticipation is earlier or worse disease each generation, a feature of triplet-repeat disorders (Block 1, 02 - Genetics); this is a point change, and the ages do not fall steadily.
  • C - affected relatives across generations on one side fit autosomal dominant hereditary cancer, which the lecture's red flags describe.
  • D - Audrey is the affected relative the lecture says to test first; once her mutation is known, relatives can be offered predictive testing.
  • E - X is a stop, not xanthine, which is not an amino acid.

stem: A healthy 30 year old woman has a family history of colon cancer affecting her father who was diagnosed at age 50, had a recurrence, and died at 70 years, her paternal grandfather who was diagnosed at 45 years and died at 50 years, and her paternal uncle, who was recently diagnosed at 60 years. She wants to have genetic testing to determine if she is at risk. You would:

options.html: Offer testing with a colon gene panel
Tell her to have her uncle tested first
Suggest that testing be deferred unless she develops colon cancer
Tell her not to worry since she is still young
Reassure her that she is not at risk since the cancer only affects males in her family.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

The accepted approach is to have the relative who is still alive, and most recently diagnosed with the cancer to be tested, given that he has already developed cancer and is likely to display the genetic abnormality. The 30 year old woman can then make an informed decision about testing depending on whether or not a recognized abnormality is present in her family.

stem: Your 68 year old patient has a non-resolving lung consolidation for which your differential diagnosis is lung cancer versus chronic pneumonia. The patient is a smoker, and her past medical history is significant for colon cancer (2 years ago) and renal cell carcinoma (18 years ago). What information should you include in the pathology requisition?

options.html: Differential diagnosis of lung cancer vs pneumonia; smoking status; history of colon cancer; history of renal cell carcinoma

Differential diagnosis of lung cancer vs pneumonia; smoking status; history of colon cancer. (The renal cell carcinoma is too remote to be of any relevance & does not need to be indicated on the requisition.)
Smoking status; history of colon cancer; history of renal cell carcinoma
Differential diagnosis of lung cancer vs pneumonia
None of the above; the information provided on the requisition should be limited so as not to bias the pathologist

answer:
The correct answer is A.

All relevant clinical information including any previous cancers (no matter how remote) should be included on the pathology report. The pathologist may not be able to access all the clinical information depending on where they practise, and failure to be provided with clinical details is a recognised source of error in pathology. Depending on the clinical history and clinical differential diagnosis, the pathologist may order additional tests on the specimen that they would not otherwise order. Pathologic diagnoses are usually a result of clinicopathologic correlation; please provide all relevant information on the requisition and don’t hesitate to call the pathologist if the case is unusual or if the report doesn’t seem to fit with the clinical scenario.

stem: A 65 year old man complains of difficulty walking for the last 2 months. He has been stumbling frequently while walking and has had a few near falls. He denies weakness and sensory symptoms. His symptoms have been progressively worsening over time. His medical history includes congestive heart failure, hypertension, and renal stones. He drinks two beers per night and quit smoking years ago. His examination demonstrates full power in his upper extremities, slight bilateral hip flexion weakness, and slight dorsiflexion weakness of his ankles bilaterally. His reflexes are normal in his arms and hyperreflexic his legs. His plantar responses are upgoing bilaterally. Pin prick sensation is unremarkable. Vibration sensation is impaired diffusely over the legs. Gait is wide-based and unsteady. What is the best localization for his symptoms and signs?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

From 10 - Introduction to Neurofunction. First step: CNS or PNS. Leg hyperreflexia and upgoing plantars are upper motor neuron signs, so the lesion is central. Second step: the pattern. Weakness confined to both legs (paraparesis) localizes to the thoracic cord or lumbar roots; normal arm reflexes and power spare the cervical cord, and impaired leg vibration fits a cord lesion below the arms.

  • A - brainstem gives cranial nerve signs and usually affects the arms too.
  • B - a cervical lesion causes quadriparesis with arm UMN signs.
  • D - lumbar roots are LMN: reduced reflexes, no Babinski.
  • E - peripheral nerves are LMN too: hyporeflexia and atrophy, not hyperreflexia.

stem: A patient is involved in a car accident, whereby she rear ends a parked car on the right. She claims she did not see the parked car. Her family is worried about her, and so they take her to the ER. The emergency physician notes that the patient cannot count fingers in the right hemi visual field when either the right or left eye is closed. What is the best localization for her problem?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

From 10 - Introduction to Neurofunction. Impaired vision in the right hemifield of both eyes localizes behind the optic chiasm, since after the chiasm each optic tract carries the opposite hemifield from both eyes. The right hemifield travels on the left, ending in the left occipital lobe. She missed a car on her right for exactly this reason.

  • A, B - retina and optic nerve are anterior to the chiasm, giving loss in one eye only.
  • C - a chiasmal lesion hits the crossing fibres from both nasal retinas, taking out both temporal fields rather than one hemifield.
  • E - the right occipital lobe processes the left hemifield.

stem: Mr Sandos is an 84 year old male that was recently diagnosed with mild vascular dementia after a stroke. He also has a history of diabetes and hypertension. He lives with his spouse, who has had to take over doing the finances and medication administration due to a few mistakes. His spouse has always done the cooking and cleaning. He is independent with his basic ADLs. He ambulates with a cane and has had one fall over a sidewalk edge in the last year. What is Mr Sando’s clinical frailty score?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

From 08 - Frailty and Falls. The Clinical Frailty Scale turns on dependence. CFS 5, mildly frail, is more evident slowing with help needed for higher-order IADLs while basic ADLs remain independent. Mr Sandos's spouse has had to take over finances and medications because of his mistakes, he is independent in basic ADLs, and he walks with a cane after a fall. The lecture also notes that frailty corresponds to the degree of dementia, and his is mild.

  • A (3) - managing well means controlled medical problems and no dependence at all.
  • B (4) - vulnerable means not dependent on others for daily help; he now is, for IADLs.
  • D (6) - moderately frail needs help with all outside activities and housekeeping, stairs and bathing; his basic ADLs are intact.

Cooking and cleaning do not count against him: 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment says to judge change, and his spouse always did those.

answer:
The correct answer is B, F, I.

Suicide attempts are more frequent and more lethal in the older adult population with depression. stem: Ageism is prevalent in North American society. Which of the following are common ageist beliefs that impact the care of older adults? Pick all that apply:

answer:

From 01 - Healthy Aging vs. Disease. Ageism is negative (or positive) stereotyping, prejudice or discrimination on the basis of age. The lecture's examples in care are clinicians under-treating illness as “normal aging” and patients under-reporting symptoms for the same reason. The keyed options are stereotypes of that kind:

  • A - “older adults overuse the system” frames their care as a burden.
  • C - “poor historians” leads clinicians to discount what the patient reports.
  • B - not a common ageist belief; if anything substance use is assumed to be a younger person's issue.
  • D - a statistic about living arrangements, not a belief.
  • E - as worded, the opposite of the ageist assumption, which is that illness is an expected part of aging.

stem: John is a 70 year old male on multiple medications. He takes a blood pressure pill three times daily with meals. He takes a cholesterol pill and sleeping pill at bedtime. He takes a water pill at 8am and 2pm. He takes a calcium and vitamin D supplement in the morning with his thyroid pill. Recently he’s been experiencing nausea and describes having a difficult time remembering to take all of his medications. What change can you make to improve John’s medication adherence?

options.html: Take all medications on an empty stomach to avoid nausea
Switch to name-brand medications as they have fewer side effects
Space administration through the day to avoid drug-drug interactions
Switch blood pressure medication to a once daily formulation

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Simplifying this very complicated medication regime is the first step to improve medication adherence. This can be achieved by switching to once daily formulations where possible. Name-brand medications have no fewer side effects than generic brands. Using a new drug to treat a potential side effect of medications only complicates the regime further (creating a prescribing cascade)

stem: Which of the following statements regarding the principles of pharmacodynamic is FALSE?

options.html: Intracellular enzymes and cell membrane transport proteins can act as receptors for drugs
A partial agonist can act as an antagonist in the presence of the receptor full agonist
A competitive antagonist can bind to the same or to an allosteric site as the agonist
Drug tolerance can be caused by a reduction in the number of receptors upon continued treatment
A non-competitive antagonist affects the efficacy of an agonist

answer:
The correct answer is C.

By definition, a competitive antagonist competes with the agonist for the same binding site in the receptor. On the other hand, a noncompetitive antagonist can bind to the same or to an allosteric site of a receptor as the agonist. If the antagonist binds irreversible to the same binding site as the agonist, the agonist won’t be able to displace the antagonist. Therefore, although binding to the same site, there is no competition. A non-competitive antagonist can also bind to an allosteric site, changing the conformation of the receptor in a way that impairs its activation by an agonist. A competitive antagonist decreases the potency of an agonist while a non-competitive antagonist decreased the efficacy of an agonist. B – in the presence of a full agonist, a partial agonist can act as an antagonist as it competes with the agonist for the receptor site but can’t promote the maximum effect.

stem: Asthma, a common condition among children, is characterized by the constriction of the airways manifested as wheezing and difficulty breathing. Which of the following route of administration would be preferred method of drug delivery for an acute asthma attack?
answer:
The correct answer is E.

The oral route would require longer time to onset and while onset may be quicker with sublingual than oral it is still slower than inhaled. Both intravenous and intramuscular routes are invasive and require special expertise and preparations. In the case of all routes other than inhaled, the drug would be seen by the entire body and not primarily the lung, which is the target organ.

stem: Which of the following statements represent a disadvantage of the intravenous route compared to oral administration of drugs? Select all that apply.

options.html: The bioavailability is greater with intravenous than oral administration
Intravenous administration bears risk of additional infection
Drugs act more rapidly when given intravenously than orally
Intravenous drug preparations tend to cost more than oral preparations
The dose of a drug administered intravenously needs to be higher than the one administered orally

answer:
The correct answer is B, D.

IV bioavailability is considered 100% which is always greater that oral bioavailability. All parenteral routes bear the risk of infection as they are invasive. Since IV drugs bypass the absorption phase, the effects can be seen faster than for oral drugs. In general, an IV preparation will cost more than a tablet of the same drug. As IV drugs bypass absorption, the dose is smaller compared to the same drug given orally.

stem: Neonatal jaundice is a condition in the newborn that arises due to breakdown of foetal haemoglobin and immaturity of glucuronidation in the newborn liver. If this newborn requires therapy with a drug that is subjected to Phase II metabolism reactions, what would be a potential consequence of the impaired glucuronidation for therapy?

options.html: There would be no consequences for therapy
The therapy would be less effective because the drug would be excreted more rapidly
This drug could potentially accumulate in the body
This drug could lose its ability to cross the blood brain barrier
The therapy would be less effective because the drug wouldn’t be converted into its active form during first-pass metabolism

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Phase II metabolism reactions (glucuronidation included) usually convert drugs into inactive metabolites that are more water soluble. In the presence of impaired or immature glucuronidation, this drug could potentially accumulate in the body because it wouldn’t be efficiently converted into the water-soluble metabolites that are excreted in the urine. One of the factors that determines the ability of a drug to cross the BBB is its lipophilicity. Phase II reactions decrease the lipophilicity of drugs. An impaired glucuronidation could result in the accumulation of metabolites that would cross the BBB more easily than the final product. First-pass metabolism is mainly accomplished by the Phase I enzymes (CYPs). This is well known for the drug chloramphenicol and the Grey Baby Syndrome which resulted from accumulation of the antibiotic chloramphenicol due to high dosing and immature glucuronidation, causing accumulation of chloramphenicol and resulting in cardiac failure.

stem: Changes in the components of ADME are most likely in which of the following populations?

options.html: Adults with early onset liver disease
The very young and the very old

answer:
The correct answer is D.

There are minimal changes in drug elimination in early onset liver disease or in the perimenopausal region, and while smoking can induce metabolism of some drugs overall there is little difference in clearance for most drugs. The most prominent changes in ADME are in the very young and very old, primarily being impactful in the areas of metabolism and excretion.

lectureMeta: The week's Self-Assessment, as it was released.
stem: Which of the following statements is CORRECT?

options.html: For drugs binding to the same pharmacological target, the most potent is the one that requires the lowest dose to cause its maximal effect
Drugs that bind to the same pharmacological target are equally efficacious
Drugs with a wide therapeutic window are more prone to cause adverse effects
For drugs with narrow therapeutic window, the ED50 will not cause adverse effects
The time to achieve a steady state concentration is longer for drugs with a narrow therapeutic window as smaller, more frequent doses are required

answer:
The correct answer is A.

The potency of a drug is related to its affinity to its receptor. Potency is represented by the EC50 which is the concentration at which the drug elicits 50% of its maximal response. The lowest the EC50 of a drug or the lowest the concentration to achieve its maximal effect compared to other drugs in the same class, the highest its potency. Drugs that target the same receptor can present completely different efficacies. The efficacy is a reflection of the conformational changes a ligand can promote to a receptor, which can vary considerably from ligand to ligand. Drugs with a narrow therapeutic window are more prone to cause adverse reactions as the different between the minimal effective concentration and the minimal toxic concentration is small compared to drugs with a wide therapeutic window. For drugs with a narrow therapeutic window, the dose at which 50% of the population responds (ED50) can certainly cause adverse effects in some individuals. This is also true for drugs with a wide therapeutic window. A drug with a narrow therapeutic window may require smaller, more frequent doses to avoid peaks of plasma concentrations that are too close to or above the MEC. However, the time to achieve the steady state concentration is dependent on the half-life of a drug, which is independent of the size of the dose.

stem: Repaglinide is an antihyperglycemic drug that is metabolized by the liver into inactive metabolites that are eliminated primarily in the feces. Which of the following would be expected if a patient taking this drug develops severe liver failure? Select all that apply.

options.html: If the dosage and/or dosing interval are not adjusted, the plasma concentration of repaglinide could achieve toxic levels
The half-life of repaglinide would be increased
If the dosage and/or dosing interval are not adjusted, the plasma concentration of repaglinide at the site of action would be lower
The new steady state concentration of repaglinide would fall below the therapeutic range
Dose adjustment would not be required as the liver impairment would not affect the active form of the drug

answer:
The correct answer is A, B.

The half-life of a drug is dependent on the volume of distribution and clearance. Since the excretion of repaglinide is heavily dependent on hepatic metabolism, its half-life would increase as a result of decreased clearance. The accumulation of the active form of this drug could result in adverse effects as the plasma concentration may achieve toxic levels if dosage and/or dosing interval are not adjusted. The accumulation of repaglinide on its active form would result in higher plasma concentrations at the site of action. The new steady concentration would fall within the therapeutic range and potentially achieve the toxic levels. The dose adjustment or even discontinuation of this drug would be required not because of lack of efficacy but because of toxicity.

stem: Aminoglycoside antibiotics are commonly used in the therapy of very ill patients. Many very ill patients also have renal compromise and the aminoglycoside antibiotics are essentially entirely eliminated via the kidney. How would one alter therapy in a patient with serious renal impairment who needs aminoglycoside antibiotic treatment?

options.html: Would not alter therapy as the infection must be controlled
Decrease dose and give less often
Decrease dose and give at same interval
Use the same dose, give less often
Use a larger dose but give much less often

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Aminoglycosides are very toxic in overdose so adjustment in renal failure is essential. Decreasing dose makes them less effective as antibiotics. Giving the same dose at a less frequent interval allows the diseased kidneys more time to eliminate the drug. Giving a much larger dose may be toxic.

stem: Mrs. Stephanec, our patient of the week, suffers from lower back pain. She was prescribed Tylenol 3, 1-2 tablets q4-6h PRN to help control the pain. Her current medications include: • Ramipril, 5mg daily • Alendronate, 70mg weekly • Cholecalciferol, 1,000mg daily • Donepezil 10 mg daily • Ibuprofen, 600 mg TID • Paroxetine, 40 mg daily • Tums, a few tablets taken PRN Mrs. Stephanec continues to complain about her pain despite taking Tylenol 3 and is showing symptoms of impaired renal function. In this case, which of the following should not be recommended in a therapeutic plan for Mrs. Stephanec’s poorly controlled back pain?

options.html: Consider prescribing other non-NSAID, non-opioid medications for her back pain
Replace Tylenol #3 with another opioid medication that doesn’t require bioactivation (e.g. morphine) on an as-needed basis
Reduce dose of paroxetine or replace it with another antidepressant

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Mrs. Stephanec is already at maximum recommended doses of ibuprofen and it is already causing renal impairment. For answer B, medications other than NSAIDs and opioids could alleviate the pain without causing the renal impairment and interactions. For answer C, opioids are recommended for acute pain but their chronic use may be concerning. For answer D, paroxetine inhibits CYP2D6-mediated bioactivation of codeine to morphine, so lowering dose can reduce enzyme inhibition.

stem: A 14 year old teenage girl with a history of epilepsy, and good response to a stable dose of carbamazepine (an anti-epileptic drug) suddenly develops seizures and requires a visit to the ER. Which of the following is NOT a potential explanation for these breakthrough seizures?

options.html: The plasma concentration of the drug may have decreased below therapeutic levels due to failure to increase the dose to account for the growth spurt
Poor adherence to drug treatment may have led to lack of therapeutic effect
Recent use of St John’s wort (a naturopathic herb that can induce CYP activity in the liver) led to an increase in the clearance of the anti-epileptic drug (i.e. to lower plasma levels)
Treatment with minocycline (an antibiotic that can inhibit CYP metabolism in the liver) lead to a decrease in liver clearance of carbamazepine (i.e. to higher plasma levels)
Use of a topical high-potency steroid (e.g. clobetasol) for 2 weeks for eczema led to CYP induction and decreased carbamazepine plasma levels

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Carbamazepine is metabolized in the liver mainly by CYP3A4, inhibition of CYPs by minocycline would lead to higher (i.e. not sub-therapeutic) carbamazepine plasma levels, and possibly toxicity (but not therapeutic failure, as described in the case). All other options are possible explanations for therapeutic failure (growth in a teenager should usually be accompanied by dose adjustments to avoid a fall in therapeutic levels in plasma; poor adherence is common at any stage of life, but seems more common in adolescence; St John's wort, and strong steroids like clobetasol (which can be absorbed and have systemic effects even if applied topically), can induce CYP expression, increasing carbamazepine clearance.

stem: A baby is born with renal tubular dysgenesis (you do not need to know what this condition is to answer this question). This is an autosomal recessive condition which can be caused by loss-of-function mutations in the gene that encodes angiotensin- converting-enzyme. This enzyme converts angiotensin I into angiotensin II. What clinical manifestations are expected as a result of this mutation?

options.html: The baby should have very low blood pressure.
The baby should have a large blood volume.
The baby might suffer from chronic hypernatremia.
The baby will have chronic hypertension.
There will be excessive aldosterone in the bloodstream.

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Angiotensin II is an intermediary in the RAAS pathway, which increases blood pressure by vasoconstriction, signals the release of vasopressin from the hypothalamus, and signals the release of aldosterone from the adrenal cortex. Aldosterone then signals the kidneys to reuptake sodium and water from urine. In the absence of angiotensin II, low blood volume and low blood pressure will result.

stem: Taylor is stranded in the desert and is in urgent need of a water source. Her blood pressure has become notoriously low and she is at risk of shock. Which of the following are increased as DIRECT result of high blood osmolarity?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Vasopressin is activated when osmolality is high or when there is low blood volume, which leads to increased permeability in the kidney and water being retained in the blood to preserve blood volume. Angiotensin II and Aldosterone are part of the RAAS pathway that is initiated when the kidney detects low blood pressure. Angiotensin II leads to vasoconstriction, and aldosterone leads to the kidney reabsorbing sodium and water from urine). Atrial Natriuretic Peptide is secreted from the atria of the heart when the blood pressure is too high as monitored by stretch receptors. This consequently leads to sodium and water leaving the body (through the kidneys), reducing the blood pressure.

stem: The autonomic nervous system is associated with the regulation of blood pressure. Which statement below is true?

options.html: When the parasympathetic nervous system receives signals from baroreceptors in the aorta and carotid arteries it will result in vasoconstriction.
The sympathetic nervous system increases stroke volume and decreases heart rate.
The tonic activity of the sympathetic nervous system increases as a result of increased blood pressure
The parasympathetic nervous system decreases blood pressure by increasing the stroke volume.
The constriction and dilation of blood vessels is controlled exclusively by the sympathetic nervous system.

answer:
The correct answer is E.

Innervation of blood vessels by the sympathetic nervous system causes constriction. The parasympathetic nervous system does not directly cause vasodilation, but activation of the PNS shuts down the SNS, allowing for reduced vasoconstriction, or vasodilation.

stem: Which of the following are plausible mechanisms that will decrease mean arterial blood pressure?

options.html: Up-regulating Sympathetic innervation to the heart
Down-regulating Parasympathetic innervation to the heart
Down-regulating Sympathetic innervation to the arterioles
Up-regulating Parasympathetic innervation to the arterioles

answer:
The correct answer is C.

By decreasing sympathetic innervation to the arterioles, blood vessels can dilate, thereby reducing total peripheral resistance and decreasing mean arterial blood pressure. Arterioles do not have parasympathetic innervation. Increasing sympathetic innervation to the heart or decreasing parasympathetic innervation to the heart will both lead to an increase in the heart rate, increasing cardiac output and thereby increasing mean arterial pressure.

stem: Which of the following does NOT correctly describe a stage of the inflammatory response?

options.html: Recognition: An offending agent is recognized by host cells and molecules
Recruitment: Leukocytes and plasma proteins are recruited from circulation
Regulation: The leukocyte and proteins are activated and eliminate the offending agent
Resolution: The damaged tissue is repaired

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Regulation involves controlling and terminating the inflammatory response. The definition given in this answer best applies to the “removal” stage of the inflammatory response.

stem: Taylor recently suffered a severe myocardial infarction and has been recovering at home for the past 6 months. Which of the following would you expect when examining her heart?

options.html: Her heart would have scar tissue deposition and would likely function as it had prior to the MI
Her heart would have scar tissue deposition and would have diminished myocardial function in the region of the MI
Her heart would undergo regeneration and would likely function as it had prior to the MI
Her heart would undergo regeneration and would have diminished myocardial function in the region of the MI

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Cardiac myocytes have very limited regenerative capacity; thus scar tissue is deposited at the site of major injury and this often leads to less-than-optimal functioning.

stem: Taylor recently suffered a severe myocardial infarction and has been recovering at home for the past 6 months. Which of the following would you expect in Taylor’s remaining cardiac myocytes after an extended period of time?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Remaining cardiac myocytes have very limited regenerative capacity, thus hyperplasia is not a viable repair mechanism following myocardial infarction. Cardiac myocytes may experience hypertrophy to compensate for the loss in function in the infarcted area.

stem: Which statement concerning the layout of the cardiovascular system is false?

options.html: Veins carry blood toward the heart
There are three layers to both veins and arteries
Arterioles and venules connect via capillaries
More blood volume exists in arteries than in veins

answer:
The correct answer is D.

While D is true most of the time, by definition, arteries carry blood away from the heart. Pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

stem: Key Feature Question: In which organs are wastes broken down or removed from the blood? (the number of correct answers is intentionally not given, should be given on a test)
answer:
The correct answer is B, C, F, G, I.

All of these organs have a role in removal of wastes: Lungs remove CO2; Lymph nodes digest pathogens; The liver processes waste metabolites; the spleen removes aged red blood cells; the kidneys remove wastes from the blood.

stem:
There are several different systems in the human body and all need to be supplied with blood. Which statements below are true? i) Endocrine signaling involves secreting hormones into the bloodstream and therefore is a slower signaling pathway than other direct methods.

  1. More red blood cells enter splenic arteries compared to splenic veins.
  2. Half of lymph returns to the cardiovascular system through the right lymphatic duct
answer:
The correct answer is D.

When hormones are secreted into the bloodstream, they return to the heart through veins, then to and from the lungs, and then from the heart to its target organs. This indirect signaling is slower than other direct methods such as nerve impulse propagation, for example. Spleens are the site of red-blood cell digestion, after about 120 days of activity. The Right Lymphatic duct brings lymph from half of the head, and the right side of the thoracic and abdominal cavities. However, lymph from the lower extremities and pelvic cavities re-enters circulation only via the thoracic duct.

stem: The autonomic nervous system is subdivided into two divisions: the sympathetic nervous system and the parasympathetic nervous system. Which statement below is true?

options.html: The sympathetic nervous system branches from the spinal cord using cranial and thoracic nerves.
The parasympathetic nervous system innervates the gut to halt digestion.
At least some portion of all pre-synaptic nerve fibres in the sympathetic nervous system are localized inside the sympathetic chain.
Parasympathetic nerves have a short pre-synaptic fiber and a long post-synaptic fiber.
Referred pain above the pelvic pain line reaches the central nervous system through the parasympathetic nerve pathways.

answer:
The correct answer is C.

All four nerve pathways in the sympathetic nervous system involve a pre-synaptic nerve fiber in the synaptic chain. In pathways 1,2 and 3, the synapses occur in the sympathetic chain. In pathway 4, the pre-synaptic nerve fiber passes through the sympathetic chain, synapsing in the paravertebral ganglia.

stem: Which option correctly describes a component of the nervous system?

options.html: The dorsal rami are associated with the skin and deep muscles of the back.
The ventral root contains afferent and efferent nerves.
Interneurons are a part of the reflex arc and allow for quick conduction of nerve impulses to the brain and back.
The Vagus nerve is a major nerve of the sympathetic nervous system.
In times of distress, salivation is halted by sympathetic nerves leaving the spinal cord through cranial nerve pairs

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Dorsal rami innervate the skin and deep muscles of the back. Ventral roots contain only efferent nerves. Interneurons do not involve brain processing but by-pass the brain. The Vagus nerve is associated with the parasympathetic nervous system. Sympathetic nerves are thoracolumbar, not cranial.

stem: Which of the following best explains the route in which the sympathetic nervous system is able to innervate the face?

options.html: A pre-ganglionic nerve originates from the Intermediolateral horn of the spinal cord at the T1 level and then synapses with the post ganglionic neuron in the sympathetic trunk at the cervical ganglia.
A pre-ganglionic nerve originates from the Intermediolateral horn of the spinal cord at the T1 level and then synapses with the post ganglionic neuron in the sympathetic trunk at the same level
A pre-ganglionic nerve originates from the Intermediolateral horn of the spinal cord at the C1 level and then synapses with the post ganglionic neuron in the sympathetic trunk at the same level
A pre-ganglionic nerve originates from the Intermediolateral horn of the spinal cord at the C1 level and then synapses with the post ganglionic neuron in the sympathetic trunk at the cervical ganglia

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Sympathetic innervation from the intermediolateral horn only occurs in the T1-L3 region of the spinal cord and to innervate higher or lower structures, the preganglionic neuron synapses with the post ganglion neuron at a different level in the sympathetic chain.

stem: Taylor is experiencing severe diffuse pain on the surface of her upper leg and groin area (innervated by spinal nerves from S2-S4). After a physical exam, the doctor ruled out somatic leg pain. Which of the following internal structures should the doctor consider in this scenario?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

The pelvic pain line corresponds to the lower limit of the peritoneum. Structures directly above it (uterus in women and the superior surface of the bladder in men) are innervated by the TLL-12 region, while structures below (cervix and male genitals) are innervated by S2- 4.

stem: An amateur analyst looks at the preliminary data of a new screening program and notices that patients who are screened have longer survival (defined as the time from disease detection to death) than those who did not undergo screening. He concludes the screening program is effective and should be instituted. Which of the following biases is most applicable to this situation?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Lead-time bias refers to a phenomenon where early detection of a disease in an asymptomatic patient falsely appears to extend the length of survival, in comparison to a patient whose disease is detected only after symptoms develop.

stem: Taylor recently had a biopsy of a tumour on her right breast – the pathologist reports a highgrade carcinoma. What does this mean?

options.html: The tumour cells are confined by the basement membrane
The tumour cells will spread to lymph nodes
The tumour cells are highly abnormal relative to their tissue of origin
The tumour has a well-organized architecture

answer:
The correct answer is C.

The grading of a neoplasm refers to how well it histologically (microscopically) resembles the normal tissue from which it originates. High grade carcinomas usually show loss of the normal architectural patterns and also abnormal looking cells – this cellular change is called “pleomorphism”. Invasive carcinoma means a tumour has broken through the basement membrane. Although many high grade tumours will spread to lymph nodes or other parts of the body, this cannot be inferred from the statement in the question stem.

stem: A physician receives a pathology report indicating that her patient has a tumor with staging T2N1MX. Which statement below is true?

options.html: The tumour is almost certainly high grade as low grade tumours do not spread to lymph nodes
The cancer has spread to non-regional lymph nodes
The tumour shows a positive resection margin
Based on the findings of the pathological report, we do not know if metastasis has occurred
The tumour has shown distant spread and cure is not possible

answer:
The correct answer is D.

The “X” after the M in the TM staging system means that metastasis is unknown based on this pathologic resection. In this system, T refers to the tumour, usually its size or depth of invasion depending on the organ involved, N refers to the lymph-node status, and M refers to metastasis. In most organ systems, non-regional (distant) lymph nodes affect the M category.

options.html: A breast cyst is usually filled with fluid or air
Fibrocystic change is indicative of a neoplasm
A fibroadenoma is a neoplasm of the breast

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Fibrocystic change may be a result of cysts and/or fibrous tissue development leading to lumpy breasts, but it is not a tumour or neoplasm.

stem: Wendy, a 47-year old mother of two teens comes to your practice concerned about a lump in her breast. Her dad was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer at age 75 and passed away shortly thereafter. What one of the following would you tell your patient?

options.html: Tell the patient that we should immediately start aggressive treatment options.
Reassure the patient that lumps in the breast do not always indicate cancer, and further testing is needed
Advise the patient that her father’s pancreatic cancer may have metastasized to her during fertilization.
nform her that the tumour present is a high-grade carcinoma which can be treated hormonally.
Write a doctor’s note to excuse her from work and tell her to rest for a few days.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

A breast lump may mean a malignant tumour, but it may also be a fibroadenoma, cyst, fibrocystic change, or abscess, all of which are benign. Further testing should be done to confirm a diagnosis. A and C.

answer:
The correct answer is A, C, E.

Benign breast tumours tend to be firm, mobile, and sometimes tender with the menstrual period. Conversely, breast cancers tend to be hard, immobile, irregular, fixed to tissue and consistently painless. A. FNAP is usually used for lymph nodes.

stem: A medical oncologist wants to know if a patient’s breast cancer has metastasized to their axillary lymph nodes. Which of the following biopsy type should the oncologist choose?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

FNA is the most minimally invasive procedure and can be used primarily for palpable superficial lesions in the breast, thyroid, lymph node, salivary glands. A punch biopsy is not appropriate, as this is not a skin lesion. Incisional & excisional biopsies are not the first investigations of choice since they are more invasive and require more equipment, sterile conditions and more time.

stem: Your patient Kathleen has a palpable mass in her left breast which is irregular with an associated skin lesion. She is concerned about breast cancer due to a family history of breast cancer. Which of the following investigation is not appropriate in this scenario?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Currently there is no blood test to detect breast cancer. This could be a topic for your Experiential Learning research! The other modalities could be used to obtain a diagnosis, with the best choices B & C. FNA cannot identify invasion, however if clinically there is skin involvement (invasion) from the underlying breast cancer, then it is not necessary to see invasion and an FNA may be appropriate here.

stem: Which one of the following definitions is incorrect?

options.html: A high grade tumour is fast-growing
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is given before surgical resection.
Dysplasia refers to a neoplasm that has spread to lymph nodes
Leukemia is a cancer of the bone marrow and blood
Hematogenous spread is a type of cancer spread

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Dysplasia refers to a group of cells showing an abnormal pattern of growth and maturation which is confined to the epithelium without breaking through the basement membrane, so there is no invasion into underlying tissues. Dysplasia cannot spread to lymph nodes since it has not gained access to the underlying tissues yet.

stem: Which one of the following is correct regarding The Two-Hit Theory of Cancer?

options.html: Cancerous cells must have 2 or more mutations in their genome
Receiving damage to 2 genes on the same chromosomes can produce cancer
Having damage to the same gene on both chromosomes can produce cancer
Receiving damage to the same gene 2 times can produce cancer

answer:
The correct answer is C.

If a cell receives damage to the same gene on both chromosomes this can produce cancer. The first hit can be inherited and second hit can be attained through life. C. FIT tests are usually done for CRC screening. Colonoscopy only for high-risk individuals.

stem: Gene A (which codes for your eye colour) becomes mutated and leads to your eye cells becoming cancerous. Which one of the following describes Gene A prior to becoming mutated?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

A proto-oncogene is a normal gene which when altered by a mutation becomes an oncogene. An oncogene is a mutated gene that can transform a normal cell into a cancer cell. A tumour suppressor gene is a gene that normally inhibits the cell cycle. B. The rest are all modifiable risk factors.

stem: Avery is a 35-year old female who was recently diagnosed with breast cancer. Avery received radiation prior to surgery and post-surgery chemotherapy. Which of the following statements regarding the role of each treatment is correct?

options.html: Radiation is neoadjuvant, chemotherapy is adjuvant.
Radiation is adjuvant, chemotherapy is post-adjuvant.
Radiation is adjuvant, chemotherapy is neoadjuvant.
Radiation is palliative, chemotherapy is adjuvant.

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Neoadjuvant therapy is given prior to surgery and aims to reduce the size of the tumour, adjuvant therapy is given after surgery and aims to treat micro-metastatic disease.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a typical characteristic of a screening test?

options.html: Screening tests are cheap and easy
Screening tests are for the asymptomatic population
Screening tests are done for rare problems

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Screening tests are usually done for common problems.

From 07 - Well Person Care and Screening for Cancer. The lecture defines screening in one sentence: we screen for relatively common problems in people who are asymptomatic, using cheap and easy tests, for conditions where early detection allows effective but less invasive treatment. A rare problem breaks that model - a test run on a low-prevalence population yields few true cases for the cost and many false positives.

  • A - cheap and easy: a stated feature.
  • B - asymptomatic population: a stated feature.
  • C - less invasive: stated, both of the test and of the treatment early detection allows.

stem: How do we typically screen for colorectal cancer?

options.html: We don’t screen for this; early detection does not change management.

answer:
The correct answer is C.

FIT test is used to detect human Heme in the stool.

From 07 - Well Person Care and Screening for Cancer. For average-risk adults aged 50-74 (asymptomatic, no high-risk features), the screening test is the FIT - the fecal immunochemical test, which detects human heme (sensitivity 92.3%) - repeated every 2 years.

  • A - an incisional biopsy samples a known lesion; it is diagnostic, never a screen.
  • B - the lecture does list flexible sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy every 10 years as an alternative, which is why this distractor is tempting, but it is not how the average-risk population is typically screened. High-risk patients (prior CRC or adenomatous polyps, IBD, a first-degree relative, FAP or Lynch) sit outside this program altogether.
  • D - false: CRC is on the screening schedule precisely because early detection changes outcomes.

stem: Which option below does not describe the best practices for screening for cancer?

options.html: Cervical cancer for low-risk individuals is screened for using a Pap test
Colorectal cancer for low-risk individuals is screened for using a Fecal
Breast cancer for low-risk individuals is screened for using a mammogram
Prostate cancer for low-risk individuals is screened for using a PSA (prostatespecific antigen) test.

answer:
The correct answer is D.

There is limited evidence that PSA screening is effective in low-risk individuals. The PSA test is specific for prostates, but not specific for prostate cancer. This screening method used on low- risk individuals will lead to many false positives.

stem: Modifiable Risk factors for cancers include everything except:
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Reproductive history is a non-modifiable risk factor.

From 05 - Cancer From Macro to Molecular. The lecture lists the modifiable (“lifestyle”) risk factors: smoking, obesity, physical activity, diet, alcohol, injection drug use, sexual history (HPV and cervical cancer) and tanning beds (melanoma). Non-modifiable factors follow the GGRAPES mnemonic, whose R is reproductive history (breastfeeding, menarche, menopause), as spelled out in the chart in 03 - Cancer Genetics.

  • A - sexual activity: modifiable, via HPV exposure.
  • C - obesity: modifiable.
  • D - tanning beds: modifiable, melanoma.
  • E - smoking: the #1 modifiable risk factor.

stem: Which statement of cancer is true for the incidence and mortality of cancer in developed countries like Canada? Choose the best answer.

options.html: The incidence of cancer is high; the mortality of cancer is high
The incidence of cancer is high; the mortality of cancer is low
The incidence of cancer is low; the mortality of cancer is high
The incidence of cancer is low; the mortality of cancer is low

answer:
The correct answer is B.

People in developed countries tend to live longer, which increases cancer incidence in general. However, better access to advanced healthcare in developed countries decreases mortality from cancer. Incidence: number of new cases in a year; Mortality: number of deaths in a year.

options.html: Cancer cells achieve limitless replicative potential through the activity of telomerase.
Cancer cells achieve self-sufficiency in growth through the mutation of protooncogenes.
Cancer cells achieve apoptosis evasion through the mutation of tumor suppressor genes.
Cancer cells achieve tissue invasion and metastasis by erupting through epithelial cells.
Cancer cells achieve sustained angiogenesis by activating an angiogenic switch.

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Mutation of tumour suppressor genes is the means by which cancerous cells become insensitive to anti-growth signals. Cells evade apoptosis by other means.

Multiple primary cancers in one person (one person has cancer left breast and

stem: Your patient comes in worried when her older sister (age, 32) was diagnosed with breast cancer. The patient’s mother had also died from breast cancer (at age 54). The patient requests a genetic testing despite being asymptomatic. Which of the following would be the next best course of action to take?

options.html: Explain to the patient how a genetic screen is unnecessary and will not change management
Arrange genetic screening for this patient
Arrange genetic screening for this patient’s sister
Arrange a psychiatric consult to address patient’s anxiety

answer:
The correct answer is C.

In this scenario, it’s best practice to confirm the presence of a mutation in an affected family member first, before testing the patient.

stem: BRCA-1 and BRCA-2 are tumour-suppressor genes. Only one functional copy of the gene is required to prevent cancer. Despite this, heterozygous carriers of a mutation in BRCA- 1 or BRCA-2 often develop cancer. Why is this?

options.html: Genetic mosaicism predisposes individuals to either ovarian cancer or breast cancer, regardless of the recessive nature of these genes.
Mutations to BRCA-1 or BRCA-2 produce variants of unknown significance; It is difficult to predict if a mutation will lead to cancer or not.
A deleterious mutation to the BRCA-1 or BRCA-2 genes in homozygotes leaves an additional copy of functional BRCA-1 or BRCA-2. Heterozygotes do not have this advantage.
Since most breast cancers are non-hereditary, BRCA-1 and BRCA-2 is not the best predictor whether a patient will develop breast cancer or not.

Due to their presence on the X-chromosome, females are more at risk of cancer arising from BRCA-1 or BRCA-2 mutations because of X-inactivation during embryonic development, and males are more at risk because they only have one X- chromosome.

answer:
The correct answer is C.

This question refers to the two-hit hypothesis. Homozygotes have an extra buffer of protection with two functional gene copies. However, with carriers of a BRCA-1 or BRCA- 2 mutation, if the single functional copy of BRCA-1/2 mutates, cancer may result (assuming other genes mutate as well)

stem: Which example below is the best example of ageism?

options.html: 87-year-old John, who is trying desperately to be admitted to a retirement home but can’t because of long waiting lists.
Recently retired 69-year-old Karen, who cannot spend as much time with her grandchildren as she would want because of COVID.
85-year-old Mabel, whose family doctor gives her overly exceptional healthcare because of her age.
84-year-old William, who has had his license recently revoked due to a delirious state.
99-year-old Harriet, who cannot secure reservations for a party celebrating her 100th birthday next week.

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Ageism can be positive or negative discrimination based on age and a patient’s status as “elderly”. The other options affect elderly patients but are not directly the result of the patient’s age.

lectureMeta: The student-written, instructor-approved bank built by the Class of 2024 Academic Directors (December 2020) and re-filed per week by the Meds 2025 volunteers.
stem: Which statement below is true?

options.html: The lifespan of Canadians has been steadily increasing over the past 20 years as a result of advanced technology.
Centenarians tend to score high on neuroticism and high on extraversion
Older adults have a decreased anti-body response, so taking the flu shot yearly is less important for geriatric patients
Age-related changes are universal, whereas disease-related changes are not
Genetics are only a small component of a long life.

answer:
The correct answer is D.

By definition, age-related changes are universal in a species. Option A is a description of life expectancy, but lifespan, the highest age reported by a species has remained unchanged since 1997. Centenarians tend to score low on neuroticism. Since elder patients have a decreased antibody response, it is more important for them to take a yearly flu shot if possible. Lastly, genetics plays a large role in living a long life.

THE FOLLOWING QUESTION STEM APPLIES TO THE NEXT TWO QUESTIONS!

You are a physician seeing a new patient, Alice. Alice is 84 years old and states that she feels

well today. Her husband passed away three years ago. She drove to the clinic today and you

noticed a sizeable dent in her car when entering the clinic. She claims that she was side-swiped

in city traffic last month. She scored [24+1] on the MoCA when completed today, losing most of

her points in the serial sevens. Her vision and hearing were recently tested and no abnormalities

were identified.

She complains of fatigue at times and the occasional headrush when standing up quickly. Past-

medical history includes three instances of post-partum depression (PPD) and has been pregnant

six times. Current medication includes over-the-counter calcium supplements (500mg) and

physician-prescribed antipsychotic sleeping pills (Seroquel, an antipsychotic), without which she

cannot fall asleep. When you question her about her ADLs and IADLs, she is mostly

independent but requires help with finances from her adult son ever since the passing of her

husband, who primarily took care of finances. She seems peppy during your interview and she

relates that her greatest pleasure is spending time with her great- grandchildren, who are 3 and 7.

She watches them during the week while her grandchildren work full- time jobs.

stem: What first intervention might you suggest to help manage this patient’s fatigue?

options.html: Ask her to complete a driving assessment
Inquire about the use of her antipsychotic medication and attempt to reduce the dose
Given her MoCA, diagnose her with dementia and begin interventions to target this
Examine her for orthostatic hypotension and treat this with medications

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Antipsychotic drugs in the elderly are associated with fatigue, weight gain, and increased CVD (among other conditions). Alice seems competent except for math-related skills (MoCA math and Finances), but we don’t have evidence of cognitive decline - in fact this seems like normal since Henry took care of finances before he died. The MoCA score is close to the cut-off, but the MoCA is not used as a diagnostic tool and Alice otherwise seems fine. Orthostatic hypotension (headrush) is an age-related change.

stem: Which of the following activities would not be considered a Basic Activity of Daily Living?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Housework is an instrumental activity of daily living.

From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Basic ADLs are the self-care tasks, DEATH: Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting/continence, Hygiene. Instrumental ADLs are the more cognitively demanding tasks of running a household, SHAFT: Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/transportation.

  • C - housework is the H of SHAFT, an IADL.
  • A, B, D - toileting, dressing and eating are all DEATH items.

The distinction matters clinically: because IADLs need more cognitive skill, they are the first to need help as cognition declines (the Clinical Frailty Scale's “mildly frail” step is defined by it).

The correct answer is D.

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Lewy Body Dementia is characterized by changes in executive and visuospatial function, visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, severe neuroleptic sensitivity, and symptoms of Parkinsonism.

cognitive domain that does not impair functional activities of daily life.
Risk factors for dementia include lower education, hypertension, and obesity.
Effective medication after a diagnosis of MCI can prevent progression toward

answer:
The correct answer is E.

There are no current medications that prevent onset of dementia after MCI. Treatments of choice are healthy lifestyle habits including exercise and diet.

stem: There are several types of dementia. Which of the following is a correct description?

options.html: Alzheimer’s dementia is characterized by amnesia, apraxia, agnosia, but normal physical exam findings.
Vascular dementia often involves weakness with decreased reflexes
Lewy-Body Dementia begins with the loss of memory, followed by executive and visuospatial functioning. Physical exam is normal.
Behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia is characterized by excessive crying at funerals and compulsive binge-eating
Language-variant frontotemporal dementia involves a dramatic increase in language proficiency at the expense of memory

answer:
The correct answer is A.

These are classic presentations of Alzheimer’s dementia. Vascular dementia involves strokes and damage to the brain which would increase leg reflex sensitivity. Lewy-Body dementia involves memory loss after executive and visuospatial function, as well as symptoms of Parkinsonism during physical exam. Frontotemporal dementia involves a normal MoCA test result, but behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia is characterized by a lack of empathy and laughing at a funeral.

stem: An 88-year old female patient has just arrived in the emergency department after a fall while you are performing an OCLO. The patient is intermittently conscious, and your attending physician asks you to perform a MoCA test. She scores 8 on the test, and you are informed by her family that she has been having trouble recalling the names of her grandchildren over the past 6 months but is otherwise functioning normally at home. She does not seem alert and gets two months correct when you ask her to recite the names of the month backwards. Based on these findings, what is at the top of your differential diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Her lack of alertness and inability to recite months of the year backwards suggest delirium. The very low MoCA score should not be seriously considered for diagnosis or screening because of its use shortly after admission into the hospital. The patient may have MCI due to trouble recalling her grand-children’s names, but the most pressing issue today is the probable delirium.

Managing well (CFS 3) refers to people whose medical problems are well-controlled, but are not regularly active beyond routine walking.

stem: Which of the following paths best describe the pathway of the upper motor neuron?

options.html: Corticospinal tract: Primary Motor Cortex -> Internal Capsule -> Medulla -> Ventral Horn in spinal cord
Corticospinal tract: Primary Motor Cortex -> Internal Capsule -> Medulla -> Dorsal Horn in spinal cord
Spinothalamic tract: Primary Motor Cortex -> Internal Capsule -> Medulla -> Ventral Horn in spinal cord
Spinothalamic tract: Primary Motor Cortex -> Internal Capsule -> Medulla -> Dorsal Horn in spinal cord

answer:
The correct answer is A.

The corticospinal tract begins in the primary cortex and traverses down the spinal tract. Efferent nerves leave the spinal tract through the ventral horns. The Spinothalamic tract begins in the spinal cord and ascends toward the brain.

lectureMeta: The student-written, instructor-approved bank built by the Class of 2024 Academic Directors (December 2020) and re-filed per week by the Meds 2025 volunteers.
stem: What of the following statements about the dorsal column tract and the spinothalamic tract are true? i) Dorsal columns transmit sensory information while the spinothalamic tract transmits motor information ii) The dorsal column tracts decussates (crosses over) at the medulla while the spinothalamic tract crosses over at the level of the spinal cord iii) The dorsal column tract and the spinothalamic tract both involve a synapse at the thalamus
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Both the spinothalamic system and dorsal column system transmit sensory information to the brain; the former transmits sensations of pain and temperature, and the latter transmits sensations of vibrations and proprioception. Both synapse at the thalamus, which relays sensory and motor signals to the cerebral cortex

stem: Which option is an accurate description of frailty or frail patients?

options.html: Frailty is a necessary and inevitable component of aging.
Frailty is the co-occurrence of multiple conditions, diseases, or illnesses.
Frailty is a syndrome associated with decreased resistance to stressors
Frail patients are more likely to be hospitalized but their hospital stays are relatively short
Patients who score CFS 9 on the frailty spectrum are completely dependent and approaching the end of life.

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Frail patients have a diminished functional reserve and reduced capacity to maintain homeostasis in the presence of stressors. Frailty is not inevitable, but frail patients are more likely to be hospitalized and have longer stays in hospitals. Lastly, CFS 9 is associated with terminally-ill patients, who have less than six months of life. The description provided is in line with CFS 8.

Elder abuse is less common if the patient is perceived as frail.

stem: In the presence of Drug B, Drug A cannot reach the maximal response regardless of dose. Which of the following is true?

Drug B has no effect on the EC50 and is a noncompetitive antagonist
Drug B affects the potency and is a reversible competitive antagonist

Noncompetitive antagonists affect the potency of an agonist but leave the efficacy unchanged.

stem: The first-pass metabolism effect refers to the phenomena that:

options.html: Parenteral (IM, SC, IV) drugs are sometimes metabolized in extracellular spaces reducing the bioavailability
Oral drugs are sometimes metabolized in the liver reducing the bioavailability
Oral and Transdermal drugs are sometimes able to attain sustained release due to slowed metabolic degradation
Most drugs are able to bypass metabolic degradation on their first pass in the body

answer:
The correct answer is B.

First-pass metabolism is when certain oral drugs are metabolized in the liver or digestive tract before absorption into the bloodstream, reducing the bioavailability (concentration of drug in circulation). Note, parenteral drugs may still be metabolized before achieving main circulation, but first-pass metabolism refers to the metabolism which occurs during oral administration.

All drugs administered intravenously will have a higher bioavailability than drugs administered orally
Elevated blood concentrations of albumin will increase the delivery of lipophilic drugs to their target tissue
Drugs entering the brain must be hydrophobic to pass the blood-brain-barrier.
The most common routes of elimination are renal excretion and biliary excretion.

stem: A half-life of a drug is estimated to be about 2 days in the human body. It also has a very large range between ED50 and TD50. Which statement below is true?

The therapeutic window changes if the dose is increased.
The maintenance dose often precedes the loading dose to establish a high plasma concentration quickly.
A patient treated with this drug would likely require rigorous analysis to avoid toxicity issues.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

As long as the total daily dose is the same, adjusting the frequency of doses will not affect the steady-state concentration of the drug. Since the therapeutic window is so large (i.e., large difference between ED50 and TD50), the patient would likely not need rigorous analysis for toxicity issues.

answer:

From 02 - Introduction to Blood Pressure Regulation. The lecture splits blood pressure control in two: the autonomic nervous system is the short-term, rapid response, and hormonal mechanisms are the long-term, slow one. A fall in pressure unloads the high-pressure baroreceptors in the aortic arch and carotid sinus, and the brain responds by raising heart rate and sympathetic tone to the arterioles - raising CO and TPR, and so MAP (MAP = CO x TPR).

  • A, D - the RAAS and aldosterone are hormonal: renin must generate angiotensin II, and aldosterone works by changing Na+ reabsorption and volume - the slow arm.
  • B - a fall in GFR is a consequence of reduced renal perfusion, and any renal volume-conserving effect is slow, not a reflex.
