answer:
The correct answer is D.

The heart is innervated by both the SNS and PNS.

From 02 - Introduction to Blood Pressure Regulation (and 06 - Adult Screening - Diagnostic Pathway for vitals). Statement by statement:

  • i - HR, RR, temperature and BP are the classic vitals; every option includes i, so the question treats it as true (06 also lists O2 saturation).

  • iii true - biological gender is on the lecture's list of factors that affect BP.
  • iv - the lecture ties TPR to vessel diameter (larger diameter = lower resistance), and lists blood volume as a separate factor in BP. It never links TPR to blood volume.
  • v false - the PNS slows HR and contractility, so the heart has both SNS and PNS supply (the PNS just does not innervate the blood vessels).

stem: Which of the following is true about the interaction of the cardiovascular system with the respiratory system?

options.html: Oxygenated blood is pumped from the right ventricle to the lungs for gas exchange
Deoxygenated blood from the systemic circulation will undergo gas exchange at the lungs before returning to the heart.
Oxygen is removed from the blood and carbon dioxide is added to the blood during gas exchange
Unlike most arteries, the pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the lungs

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Deoxygenated blood from the systemic circulation is returned to the right side of the heart through the superior and inferior vena cava. This blood is transported to the lungs via the pulmonary arteries. At the lungs, gas exchange occurs: oxygen is added to the blood and carbon dioxide removed. Then the pulmonary veins will transport the oxygenated blood to the left side of the heart, which will pump the blood into the systemic circulation. Note that the pulmonary arteries and veins are sort of unique. Most veins in the systemic circulation carry deoxygenated blood and most arteries carry oxygenated blood – this is not the case for the pulmonary arteries and veins.

stem: A 55 y/o F patient presents to ER with right lower quadrant sharp abdominal pain, you measure her blood pressure to be 160/93. What is her mean arterial pressure?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

MAP=DP+1/3(SP-DP)

From 02 - Introduction to Blood Pressure Regulation. The lecture's formula is MAP = DP + 1/3 (SP - DP). Here the pulse pressure is 160 - 93 = 67; a third of it is 22.3; and 93 + 22.3 = 115.3 mmHg.

The check worth remembering: MAP is weighted toward diastolic pressure, so it always sits below the simple average of systolic and diastolic (here 126.5). The abdominal pain in the stem is a distractor; the question is pure arithmetic.

stem: Around 1am, worried new parents of a 2 month old baby have reached out to you regarding their child feeling unwell. You recall that the baby has a rare genetic condition that results in an overexpression of ion leaky channels and may induce significant solute loss from their ECF. What are you worried about in regards to their ICF/ECF volumes as well as the respective osmolarity?

options.html: ICF volume decrease, ECF volume increase, Osmolarity reduce in both.
ICF and ECF volume both decrease, Osmolarity reduce in only ICF.
ICF volume increase, ECF volume decrease, Osmolarity reduce in only ICF.
ICF and ECF volume both increase, Osmolarity reduce in both.
ICF volume increase, ECF volume decrease, Osmolarity reduce in both.

answer:
The correct answer is E.

From 01 - An Introduction to Body Fluids Regulation. The lecture's dehydration logic runs in reverse here. Losing solute from the ECF makes the ECF hypo-osmotic, so water follows its gradient into the cells: ICF volume rises, ECF volume falls. Water keeps moving until the two compartments are iso-osmotic again, so osmolarity ends up lower in both - the cells cannot hold a different osmolarity from their surroundings.

  • A, D - ECF volume cannot rise when water is leaving it for the cells.
  • B - both volumes cannot fall with no net fluid loss; water shifts, it does not vanish.
  • C - right volumes, but osmolarity equilibrates, so it cannot fall in the ICF alone.

stem: After cell death, the majority of tissues can heal by _____.
answer:
The correct answer is D.

The majority of tissue could do regeneration repair.

From 05 - Cellular Stress & Repair. After injury, tissue either regenerates (normal function restored) or is repaired by scar. Regeneration happens in tissues made of labile and stable cells when the injury is not too severe - which covers most tissues (skin and GI epithelium constantly, hepatocytes from G0). Only permanent cells (cardiac myocytes, neurons, skeletal muscle) always heal by scarring.

  • A - fibrous scarring is the fallback for permanent cells, severe injury or damaged supporting structures, not the majority.
  • B, C - hyperplasia and hypertrophy are adaptations to stress (more cells, bigger cells), not the healing outcome after cell death.

stem: A 37-year-old woman comes into clinic with a right breast lump that she is worried about because her mother died of breast cancer. What are the next 3 most reasonable steps as a physician? (Choose 3 options)

options.html: Obtain complete history and physical exam
Request thoracic MRI to stage the cancer
Order CT of head to rule out brain metastasis
Ultrasound with possible fine needle biopsy
Order full body PET scan to rule out distant metastasis

answer:
The correct answer is A, D, F.

A – Always do history and physical first unless the patient is unstable. B- MRI is almost never a good first line test. C- This is assuming it’s a cancer which it is likely not. D- Obtaining additional information is quick and may provide valuable insight about hormone levels etc. E- While this may be the best diagnostic test, we have no firm reason to suspect cancer yet. F- This is less invasive and more appropriate to first rule out common things like cysts etc. G-PET is only to stage proven or highly suspected cancers.

stem: A 50-year-old woman presents with a breast lump that has been present for several months. She also complains of night sweats which she thinks is related to her recent onset of menopause. On physical examination, you detect a firm, non-tender mass in the upper outer region of the breast. Mammogram shows a mass with irregular borders that measures approximately 3cm in size. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.html: Perform a stereotactic-guided aspiration, send for pathology
Use a large bore (21G) needle to obtain a core biopsy, send for pathology
Reassure patient that new lumps are normal in menopausal women due to fluctuating hormonal levels
Refer to surgery and oncology immediately for excision and chemotherapy

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Red flags for breast mass are present in this case (firm, non-tender, irregular borders, older age). Night sweats can be associated with menopause, but is also a B-symptom which is characteristic of malignant neoplasm. Thus, aspiration (cyst, abscess) and reassurance are inappropriate, and needle core biopsy (staging) needs to be obtained prior to surgical excision/chemotherapy initiation.

stem: A 65-year-old woman presents with a painless lump in her breast that has been slowly increasing in size over the past few months. Biopsy demonstrates atypical cells with increased mitotic rate. Which of the following terms best describes this type of cell proliferation?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

From 02 - Approach to Neoplasia. A neoplasm is an abnormal mass arising from excessive cell division and evasion of apoptosis. A slowly enlarging lump whose biopsy shows atypical cells with a raised mitotic rate is that - abnormal cells proliferating autonomously.

  • A - hypertrophy is larger cells with no new cells (05 - Cellular Stress & Repair).
  • B - hyperplasia is more cells, but normal ones driven by hormones or growth factors, not atypical ones.
  • C - metaplasia replaces one differentiated cell type with another; it adds no mass of atypical cells.

stem: Mr. M is a healthy 50 year old man who is seeing you in your family clinic for an annual check up. He is starting to notice the effects of aging on his body and asks you what he can do to ensure that he lives a long and healthy life. Which of the following behaviors would you NOT recommend to him?

options.html: Diet high in plants, nuts, and legumes

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Modifiable behaviors associated with longevity and healthy living are: avoiding smoking, having a diet high in plants, nuts, and legumes, maintaining a normal BMI, sleeping 7-8 hours per night, limiting alcohol consumption, not snacking between meals, and regular physical activity.

stem: Mrs. E is a 71 year old woman seeing you in your family clinic. She complains that recently she has noticed that she can’t hear high pitched noises, she finds it harder to read street signs at night, wakes up to pee most nights, and finds that she is constipated more often than she is used to. Which of her symptoms are normal changes due to aging?

options.html: High frequency hearing loss and night-vision loss only
High frequency hearing loss and nocturia only.
More frequent nocturia and constipation only.
Night vision loss and more frequent nocturia only.
All of her symptoms are normal changes due to ageing.

answer:
The correct answer is E.

Normal age-related changes must meet 5 criteria: cumulative over time, progressive in nature, universal, intrinsic, and deleterious. Common changes include: higher risk of orthostatic hypotension, decreased thermoregulation, higher risk of dehydration, nocturia, wrinkles and grey hair, easier to lose ambulation, vision loss (especially night vision), high frequency hearing loss, cardiac diastolic dysfunction, finding food less appealing, constipation, decreased inflammatory response, endocrine changes, and incomplete bladder emptying.

stem: Identify each activity as either an Activity of Daily Living (ADL) or an Instrumental Activity of Daily Living (IADL).
answer:
The pairings:

ActivityADL or IADL
AmbulatingADL (activity of daily living)
CookingIADL (instrumental activity of daily living)
DressingADL (activity of daily living)
EatingADL (activity of daily living)
FinancesIADL (instrumental activity of daily living)
Hygiene (bathing)ADL (activity of daily living)
Medication managementIADL (instrumental activity of daily living)
ShoppingIADL (instrumental activity of daily living)
Social engagementIADL (instrumental activity of daily living)
TelephoneIADL (instrumental activity of daily living)
ToiletingADL (activity of daily living)
TransportationIADL (instrumental activity of daily living)
TransferringADL (activity of daily living)

From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment.

  • Ambulating is the A of DEATH, a basic ADL: moving from one position to another (transfers) and walking independently. It is physical self-care, not a household task that needs planning.
  • Cooking is the F of SHAFT (Food preparation), an IADL: it needs planning, sequencing and safety judgment, not just the physical ability to feed oneself. Do not confuse it with eating, which is a basic ADL.
  • Dressing is the D of DEATH, a basic ADL: selecting appropriate clothing and putting it on.
  • Eating is the E of DEATH, a basic ADL: the ability to feed oneself. Preparing the food is a different task - cooking is an IADL.
  • Finances are the A of SHAFT (Accounting), an IADL: the ability to pay bills and manage money, a cognitively demanding task of running a household rather than self-care.
  • Hygiene is the H of DEATH, a basic ADL: bathing and grooming oneself and keeping up dental, nail and hair care.
  • Managing medications is the extra M the SHAFT note adds to the IADLs: obtaining medications and taking them as prescribed. It depends on memory and organization rather than physical self-care.
  • Shopping is the S of SHAFT, an IADL: acquiring food and clothing.
  • Social engagement is not one of the named SHAFT items, but it belongs on the IADL side by the same logic: it is a higher-order activity of living in the community, not basic self-care of the body - and none of the DEATH items (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene) covers it.
  • Using the telephone is a T of SHAFT, an IADL, along with mail, internet and email.
  • Toileting is the T of DEATH, a basic ADL: getting to and from the toilet, using it appropriately and cleaning oneself, plus continence - control of bladder and bowel.
  • Transportation is a T of SHAFT, an IADL: driving or using public transport.

The split to remember: ADLs = DEATH (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene), the basic self-care tasks; IADLs = SHAFT (Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/Transportation) plus managing medications, the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) can be remembered by the mnemonic DEAT(T)H: Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Transferring, Hygiene (Bathing). Instrumental ADLs are shopping, transportation, cooking, finances, telephone, medications, social engagement.

options.html: A patient who is hospitalized after being struck by a car but makes a full recovery
A patient who contracts Necrotizing Fasciitis and must have both his limbs amputated making them unable to walk
A patient who lives in a nursing home
A patient who is in the hospital after catching the cold and now has reduced lung capacity

MOCA test is a diagnostic test for mild cognitive impairment

answer:

stem: An 82-year-old woman presents to your clinic accompanied by her daughter, with complaints of recent falls and dizziness. She is also concerned about recent memory loss, although her daughter says she has not noticed any significant changes in her mother. You then administer a MoCA, which she scores a 28/30. Her mediations include amlodipine, alendronate, and tiotropium. What is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Alzheimer’s disease would present with both subjective and objective memory loss (subjective - endorsed by patient; objective – endorsed by daughter and <26/30 on MoCA). Stroke would have a more severe presentation with neurological symptoms. Falls is a concern in elderly and not a part of normal aging. Therefore, A is the best answer.

stem: Which of the following practices correctly follows the principles of geriatric prescribing?

options.html: Always err on the side of undertreating rather than overtreating older patients
Consider discontinuing or dose-reducing existing medications rather than treating an ADE with another medication
Start medications at a higher dose to compensate for decreased metabolism in the elderly and then make adjustments based on response
Non-compliance is rare in older populations and when it occurs it’s usually unintentional, so there’s no need to worry about it.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Reducing polypharmacy has benefits in patient safety and adherence, but it’s important not to undertreat older patients especially for common issues such as pain, hypertension, and stroke prevention (a is false). The principle of “Think drugs” tries to avoid prescribing cascades where an ADE is incorrectly attributed to a new medical problem, leading to the inappropriate use of a second drug (b is true). The principle of “Start low go slow” recommends prescribing one medication at a time at a low dose and increasing gradually (c is false). The principle of “assessing adherence” recognizes that 25-50% of older patients are noncompliant and about 75% of non-compliance is intentional (to cut costs or avoid side effects etc.) (d is false).

The pairings:

AbbreviationMeaning
POOrally
BIDTwice a day
PRNAs needed
ACBefore meal

From 05 - Principles of Clinical Pharmacology (its prescription abbreviations table).

  • PO - orally.
  • BID - twice a day; the frequency series is q.d., b.i.d., t.i.d., q.i.d. for once to four times a day.
  • PRN - as needed; 01 - Approach To Prescribing adds that a PRN order still needs a maximum frequency.
  • AC - before meals; p.c. is after meals.
  • OD - right eye, paired with O.S. (left eye) and O.U. (both eyes).

OD is the trap: it reads like “once daily”, but the lecture's once-daily abbreviation is q.d.
